verses.text: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the thing was true, even a great warfare: and he understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision.
In those days I, Daniel, was mourning three whole weeks.
I ate no pleasant bread, neither came meat nor wine into my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, until three whole weeks were fulfilled.
In the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel,
I lifted up my eyes, and looked, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose thighs were adorned with pure gold of Uphaz:

his body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as flaming torches, and his arms and his feet like burnished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.
I, Daniel, alone saw the vision; for the men who were with me didn’t see the vision; but a great quaking fell on them, and they fled to hide themselves.
So I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.
Yet heard I the voice of his words; and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I fallen into a deep sleep on my face, with my face toward the ground.
Behold, a hand touched me, which set me on my knees and on the palms of my hands.
He said to me, Daniel, you man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright; for am I now sent to you. When he had spoken this word to me, I stood trembling.

Then he said to me, Don’t be afraid, Daniel; for from the first day that you set your heart to understand, and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard: and I have come for your words’ sake.
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me twenty-one days; but, behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me: and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
Now I have come to make you understand what shall happen to your people in the latter days; for the vision is yet for many days:
and when he had spoken to me according to these words, I set my face toward the ground, and was mute.

Behold, one in the likeness of the sons of men touched my lips: then I opened my mouth, and spoke and said to him who stood before me, my lord, by reason of the vision my sorrows are turned on me, and I retain no strength.
For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? for as for me, immediately there remained no strength in me, neither was there breath left in me.
Then there touched me again one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me.
He said, “Greatly beloved man, don’t be afraid: peace be to you, be strong, yes, be strong.” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened, and said, “Let my lord speak; for you have strengthened me.”
Then he said, “Do you know why I have come to you? Now I will return to fight with the prince of Persia. When I go out, behold, the prince of Greece shall come.
But I will tell you that which is inscribed in the writing of truth: and there is no one who holds with me against these, but Michael your prince.”

footnotes.content: A word from the Lord arrives not as comfort but as weight—the burden of truth about the warfare beneath all earthly thrones. Daniel grasps that what seems like exile and subjection is really the overflow of cosmic struggles only the God-hidden see. His old name Belteshazzar means nothing now; the revelation is his true home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three weeks of mourning—not a therapeutic fast but a man's honest love for his people, heavy with prayer. In exile he weeps for Judah's wounds, and the Lord hears every tear. Grief and intercession are the language of those who refuse to forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No fine bread, no meat or wine—the signs of an ancient fast were austere and total, stripping away daily comfort to make room for God alone. For twenty-one days Daniel says no to the world's ordinary pleasures to say yes to the Lord's extraordinary nearness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Hiddekel—that great river also called the Tigris, flowing through ancient Mesopotamia—becomes the threshold where heaven breaks into earth. God often meets us by water: there is something about standing by a river that makes a man small and ready to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man in linen, adorned with Uphaz gold—a figure dressed for ministry, radiant and set apart. When the Lord sends His messengers, they come clothed in glory that declares their errand; nothing common, nothing idle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fire in the eyes, lightning in the face, brass feet steadfast—this is the language of power and presence beyond the earthly frame. What Daniel sees is not dream but reality made visible, the weight of eternity pressed into form a mortal eye can barely hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel's companions quake and flee, blind to what he sees—a parable of solitude in faith. The Lord calls some to witness what others cannot bear, and the cost is always isolation and the weight of what only you have seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His comeliness turns to corruption—beauty drained away, strength poured out, all earthly dignity undone. In the presence of divine glory, the old self dissolves, and there is no standing in your own strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hearing the voice, he falls into sleep face-down on the earth—the posture of one unmade and remade, of surrender so complete that consciousness itself yields. The Lord speaks, and a man lies prostrate, listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hand touches him, lifting him to knees and palms—a gesture of both dignity and humility. Fallen, he is raised; weakened, he is steadied. The touch says: *I have seen you; now stand, for there is more to say.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Man greatly beloved"—the Lord's messenger opens with tenderness, not fear. Even as Daniel trembles, he learns his deepest truth: not his faithfulness but his belovedness is the anchor. Stand, for you are cherished.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the first day of prayer, the answer was already in motion—a promise that every intercession is heard before we finish speaking. The humbled heart that seeks God receives hearing, though deliverance may tarry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-one days the messenger was hindered—the spiritual warfare is real and costly. But Michael comes, one of the chief princes, and the work goes forward. We rarely see the battles waged on our behalf; faith trusts what we cannot trace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The vision concerns what shall happen to Daniel's people *in the latter days*—a word stretching far beyond his own lifetime. He is a steward of promises not for his own rest but for a future he will not see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Face to ground, mute—sometimes the only response to the Lord's word is silence and the posture of listening. No defense, no question, only the old man bowing, his mouth sealed until the Lord opens it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Touched at the lips, he speaks—but even speech is a gift given, not presumed. The sorrows of the vision weigh upon him; he owns his frailty plainly, hiding nothing from the Lord who already knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "How can I, your servant, speak to you?" This is the humility of one who has truly met God—not false modesty but honest acknowledgment that he brings nothing, stands on no ground of his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Touched again, strengthened again—the Lord does not leave him empty. Each strengthening is a rehearsal: *I will give you what you need, when you need it, as long as you ask.*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be strong, yes, be strong." The double command mirrors the double touch—the Lord will not merely whisper courage but will say it twice, for those who have far to go. Peace and strength are given together; they belong to each other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The messenger must leave to contend with the prince of Persia; the prince of Greece waits beyond—realms unseen wage their wars while earthly kingdoms rise and fall. We live in two worlds at once, and the deeper one holds the shape of all the rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this promise: though the helpers seem few and the fight vast, there is *one* champion—Michael, the defender of God's people—who stands even when no one else remains. His name means "Who is like God?"; his answer is always yes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
